method_note: FAST mode. F-01 to F-14 reused with their original sources and dates (not re-fetched today). New facts read today from official Australian Government pages.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip.

Some countries won't let you enter unless your passport is valid for six months after you plan to leave that country; some airlines impose this rule themselves; it can apply even when transiting or stopping over; getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport.

If you change your family name because of marriage, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one, and the Australian Passport Office recommends booking travel in the name that is in your passport.
facts.use_note: Book the honeymoon leg in the name on the passport you will carry.

facts.claim: Get the right visa for countries you are visiting or transiting through; visa conditions often change, so check with the embassy or consulate of your destinations before every trip.

Smartraveller advises photocopying the passport ID page, visa and key documents, taking a copy and leaving one with someone you trust, keeping hard copies of online flight, accommodation and event bookings, and sharing your itinerary with friends or family.
Check if your medication is legal and available where you're going, take enough prescribed medicine to last the whole trip, and carry copies of your prescription and a letter from your doctor.
Talk to your doctor, find out health risks where you're going, and get a basic health check at least 8 weeks before you go, including recommended vaccinations.
Smartraveller says the right travel insurance is as essential as a passport for overseas travel, for every traveller.
Policies often limit each valuable item's value; check item limits and the excess.
Free credit card travel insurance often covers fewer situations with lower item limits and usually has to be activated.
Travellers must tell their insurer about all pre-existing health conditions; most policies have an age limit.
facts.use_note: Relevant to older guests and parents.

facts.claim: Medical assistance is usually the highest unexpected cost for Australians overseas, and the Australian Government cannot pay travellers' bills.
Australians, including dual nationals, should depart and enter Australia on their Australian passport.
facts.use_note: Dual-national guests: depart and return on the Australian passport.

facts.claim: Duty free limits for travellers returning to Australia: general goods, adults AUD900, under 18 AUD450; alcohol 2.25 litres; tobacco 25 cigarettes or 25g tobacco. There are no duty free concessions on tobacco or alcohol for travellers aged under 18.
facts.page_wording: If you are aged 18 years or over, you can bring up to AUD900 worth of general goods into Australia duty free. If you are under 18 years of age the limit is AUD450.
facts.use_note: Also stated on https://www.abf.gov.au/entering-and-leaving-australia/can-you-bring-it-in/categories/duty-free. These are government limits, not prices; no Nic sign-off needed. No page date shown.

facts.claim: General goods counted in the duty free limit include gifts, souvenirs, cameras, electronic equipment, leather goods, perfume concentrates, jewellery, watches and sporting equipment.
facts.use_note: Wedding favours, gifts and jewellery bought overseas count toward AUD900.

facts.claim: You can bring most personal items such as clothing, footwear and articles for personal hygiene and grooming into Australia in accompanied baggage free of duty and tax. Personal goods are free from duty and tax if owned and used by you overseas for 12 months or more, or imported temporarily; limits apply to goods purchased overseas.
facts.use_note: The page does not describe a 'proof of prior ownership' form for jewellery taken from Australia. See gaps.

facts.claim: Families coming back to Australia on the same flight or voyage may combine (pool) their individual duty free limits, but must stay together through Customs clearance; a family of two adults and two children would have a combined allowance of AUD2700. A family includes a person and their de facto partner (including same-sex couples) or a married couple, and their children under 18.
facts.use_note: Newlyweds returning on the same flight can pool.

facts.claim: If you exceed Australia's duty free limits, duty and tax apply on all items of that type (general goods, alcohol or tobacco), not just the goods over the limit. Declare excess goods and provide proof of purchase. Failure to declare can result in penalties, prosecution or visa cancellation.
facts.use_note: Keep receipts for anything bought overseas, e.g. wedding attire or rings.

facts.claim: Duty free products are subject to powders, liquids, aerosols and gels restrictions; ABF recommends packing them in checked baggage where possible, and duty free items in carry-on that do not meet Australia's carry-on requirements must be surrendered to screening staff.

There is no limit to the amount of currency (cash) you can bring in or out of Australia, but you must declare amounts of AUD 10,000 or more in Australian currency or foreign equivalent. Failure to report movements of physical currency is an offence; prosecution and financial penalties could apply.
facts.use_note: Read from the ABF page text in a search index today; matches AUSTRAC (austrac.gov.au/general-public/moving-money-overseas). Applies when entering or leaving. Relevant for couples carrying cash vendor payments.

facts.claim: Always take spare batteries and power banks with you in the cabin; never place spare batteries or power banks in checked luggage. Devices with batteries can go in checked or carry-on baggage if switched off completely (not sleep or hibernation) and protected from damage and being switched on.

Protect spare battery terminals by keeping them in original packaging, covering terminals with tape, or placing each battery in a separate plastic bag or case. Airlines may limit the number of spare batteries and power banks you can carry; check with your airline before flying.
facts.use_note: Do not quote a per-airline number.

facts.claim: Batteries under 100Wh are common in phones, laptops and cameras; 100Wh to 160Wh need airline approval; over 160Wh are prohibited in passenger baggage (except mobility aids).

It's a good idea to carry a letter from your doctor detailing any prescription medicines you are taking, including the name of the medicine, how much you are taking, and that it is for your personal use only; ask your doctor to include complementary medicines. Where possible carry the letter with your prescriptions.

Some medicines legally available in Australia, such as those containing codeine, may not be allowed in other countries or may require a permit; restrictions may also apply to complementary medicines such as vitamins and traditional medicines. If in doubt, contact the destination's embassy or consulate. The TGA cannot advise on each country's rules.

You cannot take PBS medicines overseas unless they are for you or an immediate family member travelling with you; taking PBS medicines overseas for someone else is illegal and carries penalties of up to $11,000 and/or 2 years imprisonment.
facts.use_note: Guests should not carry medicines for other guests.

facts.claim: Take enough of your medicines and medical devices for your whole trip and carry them in your hand luggage. Medicines are exempt from the 100ml limit on liquids, aerosols and gels.
